warmup.q: A worker thread is inside Thread.sleep(10_000). Another thread calls worker.interrupt() to ask it to stop. The worker catches the InterruptedException. Inside the catch block, what does Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() return?
options: true, because it was just interrupted
false, because the flag was cleared when the exception was thrown
warmup.why: Methods that throw InterruptedException clear the interrupt flag first, so inside the catch block the flag already reads false. If the catch only prints, the stop request is gone for good. That's exactly what happened to the relay, and it's why the rule is to rethrow, or to put the flag back with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). The section on where the relay's interrupt went takes it line by line.

opening:
Picture a program with a mail room. Other parts of the program drop messages into an out tray, the outbox. A helper thread, a second path of work in the same program, empties the tray and sends what it finds. When the tray is empty, it naps, then looks again. We'll call it the relay.

One day you try to quit, and the program won't stop. The main thread asked the relay to stop, and waited. The relay printed one polite line, relay interrupted, carrying on. Then it carried on, until you pressed Ctrl+C.

That bug is easy to write. Java makes you catch InterruptedException, and printing it is the quickest way to please the compiler. JDK engineers have shipped the same mistake.

Every thread in Threads from zero finished on its own, so how do you stop one that doesn't? In this lesson, we'll follow the relay through the six states of a thread's life, weigh the ways to stop it, and fix it so the request isn't lost. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a program that wouldn't quit and a relay that answered a stop request with one printed line. We walked the relay through its six states and caught it asleep in a thread dump. Then we struck out stop(), daemons and home-made flags, and fixed the relay so the interrupt survives the catch block.

Now search some Java code, your own or an open-source project, for catch (InterruptedException. Every hit should either rethrow or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). Any hit that only prints or logs is a relay waiting for someone to press quit.

Next, we'll let two RUNNABLE threads update one counter at the same time, and watch it come out wrong with no exception and no warning.

sections.h: The six states a thread lives through
sections.html:
A thread is always in one of six states, and t.getState() tells you which. They're the six values of the Thread.State enum. The easiest way to learn them is to follow one thread, the relay, from the line that creates it to the moment it ends.

First, the relay in code. The lab class OutboxRelay is our mail-room helper. It takes the next batch of messages from outbox and hands each one to publisher, the code that actually sends it. When the outbox is empty, it naps for idleMillis milliseconds (200 here). It starts life as an ordinary object:

Java
Thread relay = new Thread(new OutboxRelay(outbox, publisher, 200), "outbox-relay");
System.out.println(relay.getState());   // NEW: only an object so far
relay.start();                          // now a real OS thread, which calls run()
Kotlin
val relay = Thread(OutboxRelay(outbox, publisher, 200), "outbox-relay")
println(relay.state)                    // NEW: only an object so far
relay.start()                           // now a real OS thread, which calls run()

Before start(), no operating system thread exists and nothing has run, so getState() returns NEW. (Kotlin reads getState() as the property state. Otherwise the two versions are the same.)

start() is the call that moves the relay on, as we saw in Threads from zero. The JVM, the program that runs your Java code, asks the operating system for a real thread, and that thread calls run(). The relay checks the outbox and sends what it finds, and getState() now returns RUNNABLE.

RUNNABLE covers two cases that the JVM doesn't tell apart. The thread may be running on a core (a part of the processor that runs one thread at a time), or it may be ready to run and waiting for a free core. It covers a third case too, which we'll meet in the next section.

Sooner or later the outbox is empty. The relay calls Thread.sleep(idleMillis) and gives up its core until the time is up. A thread that waits with a time limit is TIMED_WAITING. join(ms) leads there too, and so does wait(ms), which we'll meet in a moment.

When the time runs out, or an interrupt (another thread's request to stop, more on that soon) wakes it early, the relay is RUNNABLE again and looks once more.

Waiting with no time limit is WAITING. Picture a relay fed by a BlockingQueue instead, a JDK queue whose take() method waits until there's something to take. On an empty queue, queue.take() parks the thread, that is, puts it to sleep until another thread wakes it, here by adding a message.

join(), which waits for another thread to end, waits the same way, with no time limit. So does Object.wait(), which waits for a signal from another thread (lesson 5 of this track). In fact, the main thread from the opening was WAITING the whole time it sat in relay.join().

The fifth state is about a door. Say the relay writes each sent message into a logbook that other threads share, inside a synchronized (logbook) block. Such a block is a door with one key, called a lock: only the thread holding the lock may be inside (lesson 4 of this track covers it). If another thread is already inside, the relay waits outside the door, BLOCKED. When that thread leaves, the relay gets the lock and is RUNNABLE again.

Last, run() returns or throws, and the relay is TERMINATED. That state is final. A second start() throws IllegalThreadStateException, so work that must run again needs a new thread, or better, a thread pool (a group of reusable threads, from a later track).

The figure below draws that life as a map. RUNNABLE sits in the middle because the relay keeps coming back to it: it sends, sleeps, wakes up RUNNABLE and sends again. The three waiting states differ in what ends the wait: a lock for BLOCKED, another thread for WAITING, and another thread or the clock for TIMED_WAITING.

That's a lot of claims, so let's not take my word for them. The ThreadStates demo in the Try it sends four small threads through the same moves, asks getState() at each stop and prints the answer. On JDK 21 it printed:

before start():         NEW
inside sleep(2000):     TIMED_WAITING
in a busy loop:         RUNNABLE
inside wait():          WAITING
entering a held lock:   BLOCKED
waiter interrupted, flag now false
after join():           TERMINATED

Each state showed up where the walk said it would, though the demo visits them in its own order. The extra line about the waiter's flag is a clue for later, so hold on to it.

getState() only works on a thread you hold a reference to. In a program that won't quit, you hold nothing, but you can still ask every thread at once.

try.title: Put a thread in every state
steps: Read ThreadStates below. Each show(...) call sends a thread somewhere and asks getState(). Match each one to a box in the figure.

Run it from the labs/ folder with the command below, and compare with the output in this section. Then find the extra line the waiter prints when it's interrupted out of wait(). It explains the relay's bug, as you'll see in the section on interrupts.
Now give the waiter a time limit: change monitor.wait() to monitor.wait(5_000). Predict the inside wait(): line, then run it again.

code.title: ThreadStates.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** Puts threads into each of the six states and prints what getState() reports. */ public class ThreadStates { static final Object monitor = new Object(); static volatile boolean spin = true; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread sleeper = new Thread(() -> pause(2_000), "sleeper"); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", "before start():", sleeper.getState()); sleeper.start(); show(sleeper, Thread.State.TIMED_WAITING, "inside sleep(2000):"); Thread busy = new Thread(() -> { while (spin) Thread.onSpinWait(); }, "busy"); busy.start(); show(busy, Thread.State.RUNNABLE, "in a busy loop:"); Thread waiter = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (monitor) { try { monitor.wait(); // no timeout } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("waiter interrupted, flag now " + Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()); } } }, "waiter"); waiter.start(); show(waiter, Thread.State.WAITING, "inside wait():"); Thread blocked = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (monitor) { } }, "blocked"); synchronized (monitor) { // main holds the monitor... blocked.start(); // ...so this thread cannot enter show(blocked, Thread.State.BLOCKED, "entering a held lock:"); } spin = false; waiter.interrupt(); for (Thread t : new Thread[] {sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked}) t.interrupt(); for (Thread t : new Thread[] {sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked}) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", "after join():", sleeper.getState()); } // getState() is a snapshot, so poll until the thread gets where we sent it static void show(Thread t, Thread.State expected, String label) throws InterruptedException { for (int i = 0; i < 200 && t.getState() != expected; i++) Thread.sleep(10); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", label, t.getState()); } static void pause(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: ThreadStates.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Puts threads into each of the six states and prints what getState() reports. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val monitor = Object() // java.lang.Object, because Kotlin's Any has no wait() @Volatile private var spin = true fun main() { val sleeper = Thread({ pause(2_000) }, "sleeper") println("%-24s%s".format("before start():", sleeper.state)) sleeper.start() show(sleeper, Thread.State.TIMED_WAITING, "inside sleep(2000):") val busy = thread(name = "busy") { while (spin) Thread.onSpinWait() } show(busy, Thread.State.RUNNABLE, "in a busy loop:") val waiter = thread(name = "waiter") { synchronized(monitor) { try { monitor.wait() // no timeout } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("waiter interrupted, flag now ${Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted}") } } } show(waiter, Thread.State.WAITING, "inside wait():") val blocked = Thread({ synchronized(monitor) { } }, "blocked") synchronized(monitor) { // main holds the monitor... blocked.start() // ...so this thread cannot enter show(blocked, Thread.State.BLOCKED, "entering a held lock:") } spin = false val all = listOf(sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked) all.forEach { it.interrupt() } all.forEach { it.join() } println("%-24s%s".format("after join():", sleeper.state)) } // getState() is a snapshot, so poll until the thread gets where we sent it private fun show(t: Thread, expected: Thread.State, label: String) { var i = 0 while (i++ < 200 && t.state != expected) Thread.sleep(10) println("%-24s%s".format(label, t.state)) } private fun pause(ms: Long) { try { Thread.sleep(ms) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } }

try.expect: The first run matches the section line for line: NEW, then TIMED_WAITING (the sleeper), RUNNABLE (the busy loop), WAITING (the waiter in wait()), BLOCKED (main holds monitor, so the new thread can't get in) and finally TERMINATED. The waiter prints waiter interrupted, flag now false: the interrupt woke it, and the flag was cleared on the way out. With wait(5_000), the waiter's line reads TIMED_WAITING, after a pause of about two seconds, because show keeps polling for a WAITING that never comes and then prints what it sees. Same call plus a time limit, and the thread moves to the other box.

sections.h: Reading the states in a thread dump
sections.html:
Back to the program that wouldn't quit. A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread in the JVM, with its state and its stack, the chain of method calls it's in the middle of.

jcmd <pid> Thread.print takes one. jcmd is a tool that comes with the JDK, and <pid> is the process id, the number the operating system gives each running program. Here's the relay a moment after it was interrupted, trimmed to the lines that matter:

"outbox-relay" #19 prio=5 os_prio=0 ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping)
        at java.lang.Thread.sleep0(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method)
        at java.lang.Thread.sleep(java.base@21.0.12.1/Thread.java:509)
        at workbench.concurrency.l02.OutboxRelay.run(OutboxRelay.java:39)

The dump says what the relay is doing in two places. The state line says TIMED_WAITING (sleeping), and the stack says where: in Thread.sleep, called from line 39 of OutboxRelay.run. So the relay heard the interrupt, printed that it had heard it, and went straight back to bed.

A state is a snapshot, so take two or three dumps a few seconds apart. A thread at the same line in all of them isn't just passing through.

Two states need care when you read a dump. The first is RUNNABLE, and here is the third case we put off. The Javadoc, Java's official API documentation, says a RUNNABLE thread is executing in the JVM "but it may be waiting for other resources from the operating system such as processor."

So a thread that waits for a slow web service (a program on another computer) to answer over the network often shows RUNNABLE too. The JVM only sees that it's inside native code, code that runs outside Java in the operating system. A dump full of RUNNABLE threads can still be a program that does nothing.

The second is BLOCKED, which is only for synchronized. A thread waiting for a ReentrantLock, the JDK's other kind of lock (lesson 7 of this track), is parked by the lock's own Java code. So the dump shows it WAITING, with LockSupport.park near the top of its stack. Search a dump for BLOCKED to find threads stuck behind a lock, and you'll miss every ReentrantLock.

A state is a hint. The stack is the evidence. Read both.

Our relay spends nearly all of its life in TIMED_WAITING, asleep. So the real question is how one thread can reach into another thread's sleep and ask it to stop.

sections.h: Weighing the ways to stop a thread
sections.html:
We know where the relay spends its time: asleep, or busy sending. Whatever we use to stop it has to reach it in both places. People try four ways, so let's take them in turn, oldest first.

The oldest is Thread.stop(). It threw an error inside the target thread, wherever that thread happened to be. The thread unwound, leaving every method it was in, released its locks and left half-updated objects behind. Picture half a batch sent, with those messages not yet marked as sent, so they'd go out a second time.

stop() was deprecated, that is, marked as "don't use this", in Java 1.2. It was made to always throw UnsupportedOperationException in JDK 20, and removed in JDK 26. Its partners suspend() and resume() went in JDK 23. In Java, deprecation is a long goodbye.

Old code that calls it now fails with NoSuchMethodError. Strike that one.

The second is to make the relay a daemon thread, one the JVM doesn't wait for. When the last non-daemon thread ends, the JVM exits, and daemon threads stop wherever they are, without running their finally blocks. A new thread copies the daemon setting of the thread that created it, so you change it yourself, before start():

Java
Thread relay = new Thread(outboxRelay, "outbox-relay");
relay.setDaemon(true);   // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException
relay.start();
Kotlin
val relay = Thread(outboxRelay, "outbox-relay")
relay.isDaemon = true    // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException
relay.start()            // or: thread(name = "outbox-relay", isDaemon = true) { outboxRelay.run() }

A daemon doesn't stop the relay so much as abandon it. The JVM can cut it off between sending a message and marking it sent. Daemons suit work you can afford to lose halfway, such as the metrics-flusher in the Try it below, or the JVM's own housekeepers from Threads from zero. For a mail room that must not lose or repeat messages, strike this one too.

The third is a flag of our own, a running field that the owner sets to false and the loop checks on every pass. (It has to be volatile, a keyword that makes other threads see the newest value. The memory model track, on Java's rules for what one thread sees of another's writes, explains why.) A flag works for a busy loop, but it can't wake a sleeping thread.

Our relay would notice the flag only when its current sleep ends, and a relay parked in queue.take() would never notice it at all. Thread pools, which you'll meet later, don't know about your flag either.

The fourth is interrupt(), and it's the one Java builds on. t.interrupt() sets a flag inside t, called the interrupt flag. If t is blocked, that is, waiting, in sleep, wait, join or a call such as BlockingQueue.take(), that call wakes up and throws InterruptedException.

If t is busy instead, nothing happens right away: the interrupt flag stays set until the thread looks at it. When you shut a thread pool down with shutdownNow(), it stops the running tasks this same way.

So stopping a thread in Java is cooperative. The interrupt asks. The thread checks, finishes what it's doing, cleans up and returns, at a moment when its data makes sense.

Java can't kill a thread. It can only ask, and the thread stops itself.

The interrupt is the right tool, then. But our relay was interrupted, and it carried on. Let's find out where the request went.

try.title: Lose a finally block
steps: Run DaemonDemo. Its metrics-flusher thread prints a running count every 200 ms. Count the flushes, and look for the line from the finally block.
Change setDaemon(true) to setDaemon(false) (in Kotlin, isDaemon = true to false) and run it again. Stop it with Ctrl+C once you've seen enough.
Keep it non-daemon, and add metrics.interrupt(); metrics.join(); just before main's last println. Predict the last two lines, then run it once more.

code.title: DaemonDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive. Its finally block does not run either. */ public class DaemonDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread metrics = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int i = 1; ; i++) { System.out.println("metrics: flush " + i); Thread.sleep(200); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { System.out.println("metrics: finally block ran"); } }, "metrics-flusher"); metrics.setDaemon(true); // must be called before start(); try false metrics.start(); Thread.sleep(700); System.out.println("main: done, returning"); } }

alt.title: DaemonDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 // A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive. Its finally block does not run either. fun main() { val metrics = Thread({ try { var i = 1 while (true) { println("metrics: flush ${i++}") Thread.sleep(200) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } finally { println("metrics: finally block ran") } }, "metrics-flusher") metrics.isDaemon = true // must be set before start(); try false metrics.start() // (or: thread(isDaemon = true) { ... }) Thread.sleep(700) println("main: done, returning") }

try.expect: As a daemon, you get four flushes and main: done, returning, and no finally block ran: the JVM exited underneath the thread. As a non-daemon, it flushes forever, because nothing asks it to stop. With the interrupt and the join, it stops at once and prints metrics: finally block ran before main: done, returning. That's what a clean shutdown looks like: ask, then wait.

sections.html:
Here's the part of the relay that answered the stop request, straight from the lab's starting code:

Java
// Naive: the interrupt is "handled" by printing it
try {
    Thread.sleep(idleMillis);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    System.err.println("relay interrupted, carrying on");
}
Kotlin
// Naive: the interrupt is "handled" by printing it
try {
    Thread.sleep(idleMillis)
} catch (e: InterruptedException) {
    System.err.println("relay interrupted, carrying on")
}

The catch block looks harmless: the exception was caught, and a line was printed. But methods that throw InterruptedException clear the interrupt flag before they throw. So inside the catch block the flag already reads false, which was the warm-up question.

Remember the waiter's line in ThreadStates, flag now false? That was the same clearing, caught in the act. The relay prints, loops round and calls sleep again, and nothing anywhere remembers that someone asked it to stop.

Picture the relay as a clerk in the mail room, and the interrupt as a note left on the clerk's desk: "please finish up". If the clerk is napping, the note wakes them. If they're busy sorting letters, they see it the next time they look up.

The catch is that waking up tears the note off. The note is the interrupt flag, and sleep tears it off when it throws.

Once you've caught the exception, then, you hold the only copy of the request. You have two good options. Let the exception travel up to your caller, by declaring throws InterruptedException. Or stick the note back on, by restoring the flag before you do anything else:

Java
try {
    Thread.sleep(backoffMillis);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // put the request back
    return;                               // then stop, or throw your own exception
}
Kotlin
try {
    Thread.sleep(backoffMillis)           // Kotlin doesn't force this try, so add it on purpose
} catch (e: InterruptedException) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt()    // put the request back
    return                                // then stop, or throw your own exception
}

Never swallow an interrupt. Rethrow it, or restore it.

If this feels like an easy mistake, you're in good company. JDK 23 fixed ImageIcon.loadImage to restore the flag, and JDK 24 fixed the same bug in FileSystemPreferences.lockFile(). From JDK 26, the Thread Javadoc has a section on interruption that spells out the rule above.

The relay has a second, quieter way to miss the note. When the outbox is full, it sends batch after batch and never reaches sleep, so no InterruptedException ever arrives. A loop like that must look for the note itself, once per batch, with Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted().

Be careful with the static Thread.interrupted(), which looks almost the same. It reads the flag and clears it, so use it only when you mean to take the note down for good.

With both fixes in place, the relay stops when it's asked to. The code that asks still has one job left: wait for the relay to finish, and not forever.

try.title: Watch the flag disappear
steps: Run InterruptFlag and read the five numbered lines.
Comment out the line me.interrupt() in the catch block. Predict lines 2 to 5, then run it again.
Explain to yourself why line 4 prints true with the restore in place, and why line 5 then prints false.

code.title: InterruptFlag.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** Watch the interrupt flag: set by interrupt(), cleared when sleep() throws, restored by you. */ public class InterruptFlag { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { Thread me = Thread.currentThread(); try { Thread.sleep(10_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("1. caught InterruptedException, flag is now " + me.isInterrupted()); me.interrupt(); // restore it: comment this line out and run again System.out.println("2. after interrupt(), flag is " + me.isInterrupted()); } System.out.println("3. isInterrupted() only reads it: " + me.isInterrupted()); System.out.println("4. Thread.interrupted() reads AND clears: " + Thread.interrupted()); System.out.println("5. so now the flag is " + me.isInterrupted()); }, "worker"); worker.start(); Thread.sleep(200); worker.interrupt(); // a request, not a command worker.join(); } }

alt.title: InterruptFlag.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Watch the interrupt flag: set by interrupt(), cleared when sleep() throws, restored by you. fun main() { val worker = thread(name = "worker") { val me = Thread.currentThread() try { Thread.sleep(10_000) // Kotlin doesn't force this try/catch on you } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("1. caught InterruptedException, flag is now ${me.isInterrupted}") me.interrupt() // restore it: comment this line out and run again println("2. after interrupt(), flag is ${me.isInterrupted}") } println("3. isInterrupted only reads it: ${me.isInterrupted}") println("4. Thread.interrupted() reads AND clears: ${Thread.interrupted()}") println("5. so now the flag is ${me.isInterrupted}") } Thread.sleep(200) worker.interrupt() // a request, not a command worker.join() }

try.expect: With the restore: false, true, true, true, false. Line 1 is false because sleep cleared the flag on its way out, and line 2 shows the note stuck back on. Line 4 uses Thread.interrupted(), which reads the flag and clears it, so line 5 is false. Without the restore, every line prints false. The request was lost the moment the exception was caught, exactly as in the relay.

refs.title: Thread.java at jdk-27-ga, with the "Thread Interruption" section

aside.title: Is coroutine cancellation the same thing?
aside.html: Same idea, separate machinery. A Kotlin coroutine is a light task that can pause without holding on to a thread, and the coroutines track covers them. Cancelling one is cooperative too: delay() and the other suspending functions in kotlinx.coroutines notice it and throw CancellationException. A catch (e: Exception) that swallows that exception can keep a cancelled coroutine running, much like a swallowed interrupt. But cancelling a coroutine doesn't interrupt the thread it runs on. When a coroutine must call blocking code that only listens to interrupts, wrap the call in runInterruptible { }, which turns cancellation into an interrupt. The coroutines track covers this in Cancellation and timeouts.

sections.h: Waiting for the relay to finish
sections.html:
Now look at the other side of quitting. The main thread did what the textbooks say: relay.interrupt(), then relay.join(), then close the mailer, the connection the relay sends its messages through. With the old relay, that join() waited until you pressed Ctrl+C. With the fixed relay, it returns as soon as the relay has finished the batch in hand.

You may be thinking, "Why wait at all? Interrupt it and close the mailer." Because the relay may still be sending, and closing the mailer under it makes those sends fail. The next idea is usually this one:

Java
// Naive: hopes two seconds is enough
relay.interrupt();
Thread.sleep(2_000);     // "should be enough"
mailer.close();
Kotlin
// Naive: hopes two seconds is enough
relay.interrupt()
Thread.sleep(2_000)      // "should be enough"
mailer.close()

Thread.sleep(ms) pauses the current thread for at least that long, and it promises nothing about any other thread. On a quiet laptop the relay stops within a few milliseconds, and the code works. On a computer that's busy with other programs, two seconds may not be enough.

Even when the relay finishes in time, the main thread isn't promised to see what it wrote. Java's rules give sleep no meaning for other threads. That leaves the JIT compiler free to keep a value in a register, a small storage slot inside the core, or to move a read or a write. (The JIT compiler is the part of the JVM that turns code that runs often into machine code.) The memory model track shows a loop that never ends for exactly this reason.

join() fixes both problems. It waits for the thread to end, and when it returns, you're guaranteed to see everything that thread wrote. The java.util.concurrent docs put it this way: "All actions in a thread happen-before any other thread successfully returns from a join on that thread."

Happens-before is the memory model's name for that guarantee, and it's why Threads from zero could read the partial array after the joins with no locks at all.

Plain join() has one weakness, and our program that wouldn't quit found it: it waits as long as it takes. So give it a limit.

join(5_000) waits up to five seconds and returns nothing, so you check relay.isAlive() afterwards. Since JDK 19, join(Duration) returns true if the thread ended:

Java
// Fixed: ask, then wait, but not forever
relay.interrupt();
boolean stopped = relay.join(Duration.ofSeconds(5));   // JDK 19+: true if it ended
if (!stopped) System.err.println("relay still running after 5 s");
mailer.close();
Kotlin
// Fixed: ask, then wait, but not forever
relay.interrupt()
val stopped = relay.join(Duration.ofSeconds(5))       // JDK 19+: true if it ended
if (!stopped) System.err.println("relay still running after 5 s")
mailer.close()

A timed join returns as soon as the thread ends, so it costs nothing when the relay behaves. When it returns false, you know the relay is stuck, and can decide what to do.

Keep sleep for what it's for: a pause. A back-off, the short wait before you try a slow web service again, is a pause, and so is the relay's nap between looks at the outbox.

Wait for the thread, not for the clock.

That completes a thread's life: we can start it, read its state, ask it to stop and wait for it to finish. But none of it protects data that two threads change while both are running, and that's where most concurrency bugs live.

try.title: Give up waiting, then wait properly
steps: Read JoinWithTimeout. The worker takes about 500 ms to fetch a price from a slow web service, and main waits for it twice. Predict both printed lines.
Change the timed join to fetch.join(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) and run it again. What does ended say now, and how long did main wait?

code.title: JoinWithTimeout.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; import java.time.Duration; /** join(timeout) gives up waiting; join() waits for the end and makes the result visible. */ public class JoinWithTimeout { static long priceCents; // plain field: join() is what makes the write visible public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread fetch = new Thread(() -> { sleepQuietly(500); // stands in for a slow web service that answers in 500 ms priceCents = 10_842; }, "price-fetch"); fetch.start(); boolean ended = fetch.join(Duration.ofMillis(100)); // JDK 19+: returns whether it ended System.out.println("after join(100 ms): ended=" + ended + ", alive=" + fetch.isAlive() + ", price=" + priceCents); fetch.join(); // no timeout: wait for the end System.out.println("after join(): alive=" + fetch.isAlive() + ", price=" + priceCents); } static void sleepQuietly(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: JoinWithTimeout.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import java.time.Duration import kotlin.concurrent.thread // join(timeout) gives up waiting; join() waits for the end and makes the result visible. private var priceCents = 0L // plain field: join() is what makes the write visible fun main() { val fetch = thread(name = "price-fetch") { try { Thread.sleep(500) // stands in for a slow web service that answers in 500 ms } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } priceCents = 10_842 } val ended = fetch.join(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // JDK 19+: returns whether it ended println("after join(100 ms): ended=$ended, alive=${fetch.isAlive}, price=$priceCents") fetch.join() // no timeout: wait for the end println("after join(): alive=${fetch.isAlive}, price=$priceCents") }

try.expect: First run: ended=false, alive=true, price=0, then alive=false, price=10842. The 100 ms join gave up early, and the plain join waited for the end and saw the price. With a 2-second limit, ended=true and the price is already there after about 500 ms. A timed join returns as soon as the thread ends; it doesn't sit out the full time.

compare.title: An interruptible polling loop in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: Thread relay = new Thread(() -> { Thread me = Thread.currentThread(); while (!me.isInterrupted()) { // poll the outbox and publish here try { Thread.sleep(50); // the compiler forces you to handle the checked exception } catch (InterruptedException e) { me.interrupt(); // restore the flag, so the loop condition sees it } } System.out.println("relay stopped, flag = " + me.isInterrupted()); }, "outbox-relay"); relay.start();

kotlin.title: KotlinRelay.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A polling loop that follows the interruption protocol, in Kotlin. fun main() { val relay = thread(name = "outbox-relay") { val me = Thread.currentThread() while (!me.isInterrupted) { // property syntax for isInterrupted() // poll the outbox and publish here try { Thread.sleep(50) // no try/catch is forced on you in Kotlin... } catch (e: InterruptedException) { me.interrupt() // ...but the protocol is the same: restore the flag } } println("relay stopped, flag = ${me.isInterrupted}") } Thread.sleep(300) relay.interrupt() relay.join() println("relay alive after join: ${relay.isAlive}") }

compare.note: Both versions follow the same protocol, line for line: loop until the flag is set, sleep, and restore the flag in the catch block. Two things differ. First, Kotlin has no checked exceptions (exceptions the compiler makes you catch or declare), so Thread.sleep(50) compiles with no try at all, and that changes how the bug looks. In Java the usual mistake is a catch that swallows the interrupt. In Kotlin it's often no catch at all: the InterruptedException escapes the lambda, the thread dies with a stack trace on standard error, and any cleanup after the loop never runs. Neither is a clean stop. Here Java's checked exception earns its keep: the compiler won't let you forget that interrupts exist, even if it can't make you handle them well. Second, isInterrupted reads as a property in Kotlin, while the static Thread.interrupted() still reads the flag and clears it.

steps.say: Here's a retry loop of a kind most programs have somewhere. It hands a letter to a mail server, a program on another computer that delivers it. When the server is too slow and the call times out, the loop waits a little longer each time and tries again. Read it and find the line where a stop request disappears.
steps.code: Receipt send(Letter letter) { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return mailServer.send(letter); } catch (MailTimeoutException e) { try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { System.err.println("interrupted while waiting to retry"); // and loop again } } } }

alt.html: fun send(letter: Letter): Receipt { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return mailServer.send(letter) } catch (e: MailTimeoutException) { try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt) } catch (ie: InterruptedException) { System.err.println("interrupted while waiting to retry") // and loop again } } attempt++ } }

steps.say: It's the inner catch. sleep cleared the flag before it threw, so after the printed line nothing remembers the request, and the loop has no limit. If the mail server is down when you quit, this thread retries until you press Ctrl+C. It's the relay's bug in a different place. Before you read on, decide what the method should do when it's interrupted.

Put the request back first, then stop retrying and tell the caller why. Wrapping the cause in your own exception is fine, as long as the flag is set before you throw. And while we're here, let's give the retries a limit.
steps.code: Receipt send(Letter letter) { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return mailServer.send(letter); } catch (MailTimeoutException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; // 1. bounded retries try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // 2. restore the request throw new SendCancelledException(letter.id(), ie); // 3. stop, and say why } } } }

alt.html: fun send(letter: Letter): Receipt { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return mailServer.send(letter) } catch (e: MailTimeoutException) { if (attempt == 3) throw e // 1. bounded retries try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt) } catch (ie: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // 2. restore the request throw SendCancelledException(letter.id, ie) // 3. stop, and say why } } attempt++ } }

steps.say: Now the caller, say the relay or a thread pool that is shutting down, finds the interrupt flag still set on its thread, and the letter is reported as cancelled instead of being retried forever. If send could simply declare throws InterruptedException, that would be simpler still: there would be nothing to restore.

lab.title: Make the mail-room relay stop on interrupt
steps: Open OutboxRelay, the mail-room helper from this lesson. outbox is a Supplier that returns the next batch of waiting messages, publisher is a Consumer that sends one message, and idleMillis is how long to nap when the batch is empty.
Run the tests. All five fail, and the run is slow, because each test waits 5 seconds for a relay that never stops. This is the relay from the opening.
Read OutboxRelay.run(). Find the two ways it ignores an interrupt: while sleeping, and while busy with full batches.
Change the loop condition so it checks Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() once per batch. Finish the batch in hand before checking.
Handle the InterruptedException from sleep by restoring the flag and leaving the loop.
Run the tests until all five pass, then run them once more.
hints: Put the try around the whole while loop. Then the catch block runs once, restores the flag, and run() returns.
If the loop ends because isInterrupted() returned true, the flag is still set. You only need to restore it after an InterruptedException.
The "finishes the batch" test counts messages: the total must be a multiple of the batch size. Don't check the flag inside the for loop over the batch.

drill.title: Write an interruptible poller from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a Runnable that keeps asking a Supplier<List<String>> for work and prints each item. When the list is empty, it sleeps 100 ms. It must stop when interrupted, whether it's sleeping or busy, and leave the flag set when it returns. Then compare with the answer.

answer.html: Runnable poller = () -> { try { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { List<String> batch = source.get(); batch.forEach(System.out::println); if (batch.isEmpty()) Thread.sleep(100); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // sleep cleared it; put it back } };

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: val poller = Runnable { try { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) { val batch = source.get() batch.forEach(::println) if (batch.isEmpty()) Thread.sleep(100) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // sleep cleared it; put it back } }

recap: A thread starts NEW, becomes RUNNABLE at start(), steps out of RUNNABLE to wait for a lock (BLOCKED), for another thread (WAITING) or for another thread or the clock (TIMED_WAITING), and ends TERMINATED when run() returns.

In a thread dump, read the stack as well as the state. RUNNABLE also covers waiting for a core and sitting in native I/O, and a thread parked on a ReentrantLock shows WAITING, because BLOCKED is only for synchronized.

Java can't kill a thread (Thread.stop() was removed in JDK 26), and a daemon is abandoned, not stopped. interrupt() sets a flag, and blocking calls like sleep, wait, join and take throw InterruptedException and clear it.
When you catch InterruptedException, rethrow it or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). A loop that never blocks must check isInterrupted() itself.
join() waits for a thread to end and makes everything it wrote visible to you; give it a timeout when the wait must end. sleep() only passes time.
The limit: start, interrupt and join coordinate one thread with another. They don't protect data that two running threads change at the same time.

explain.prompt: A friend asks: "Why can't I just catch InterruptedException and print it? The thread keeps working, so what's the harm?" Answer them in your own words.
explain.answer: An interrupt is how the rest of the program asks your thread to stop: shutdown code and, later, thread pools all use it. When sleep or wait throws InterruptedException, it clears the interrupt flag first. If you only print it, the request is gone, and nobody above you can tell it was ever made. So the loop keeps running, and quitting hangs until someone kills the program, just like the mail-room relay. Either let the exception travel up to your caller, or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to put the flag back, then stop what you're doing.

deeper.html:
Not every blocking call listens to interrupts, and it's worth knowing which ones don't before one surprises you.

sleep, wait, join, BlockingQueue.take and Lock.lockInterruptibly throw InterruptedException. A thread blocked on an InterruptibleChannel, from java.nio, the JDK's newer library for files and networks, gets different treatment: the Javadoc says the channel is closed, the flag is set and the thread receives a ClosedByInterruptException. So interrupting a thread that is writing to a FileChannel closes the file for everyone who shares that channel. That one surprises people.

Plain synchronized doesn't respond at all. A thread that is BLOCKED waiting for a lock stays blocked when you interrupt it; only the flag changes. A platform thread reading a classic java.net.Socket stream may also sit there until data arrives. For those, give the wait a timeout (a socket read timeout, or tryLock with a timeout), so the thread wakes up now and then and can check its flag.

Two smaller facts to finish. Interrupts are part of the memory model too: if T1 interrupts T2, everything T1 did before the interrupt is visible to T2 once T2 sees it, by catching the exception or by reading the flag. And the JDK 27 Javadoc for interrupt() notes that interrupting a thread that isn't alive still records the request in the JDK's own implementation, so don't count on an interrupt sent before start() being dropped.
